content: The unit known as kilogram-force (kgf), also referred to as kilopond (kp), is defined as the force exerted by Earth's gravity on a mass of one kilogram. This force is equivalent to approximately 9.80665 meters per second squared, or 9.80665 newtons. The kilogram-force has never been included in the International System of Units (SI), which was established in 1960. Instead, the SI unit of force is the newton. However, prior to the adoption of the SI system, the kilogram-force was widely used across many parts of the world. Even today, it remains in use for specific applications. For instance, during the 1940s in Germany, the thrust of rocket engines was measured in kilograms-force. Similarly, in the Soviet Union, this unit was the primary measure of thrust in the Russian space program until at least the late 1980s. Presently, the kilogram-force is still utilized in China and occasionally by the European Space Agency. The kilogram-force is also employed in various other contexts, such as measuring the tension of bicycle spokes, torque (expressed in meter-kilograms), pressure (in kilograms per square centimeter), the draw weight of bows in archery, and defining metric horsepower (PS) as 75 m·kgf/s. The value of 9.80665 m/s² was officially adopted for this purpose in 1901, although the unit had been used in low-precision force measurements prior to that time. A tonne-force, also known as a metric ton-force, megagram-force, or megapond (Mp), is equivalent to 1,000 kilograms-force. Additionally, the decanewton (daN) is sometimes used in certain fields as an approximation of the kilogram-force, as it is exactly 10 newtons rather than an approximate value.
